source: OpsHarness (2026) staged dual-gate verification
finding: Every proposed memory or tool change is tested in a sandbox copy. Inner gate: no accuracy loss and no cost rise on the cases it was mined from, with a strict gain in one. Outer gate: no regression on a held-out testbed that is re-sampled before each evolution, kept disjoint from the mined cases, and stratified by fault family.
numbers: Cost tolerance 0.05. Up to 3 refine-and-retry rounds, then discard. Testbed size is 'by default the evolve window' (a number not stated in the text read). 12 windows, one evolution per window.
quote: A mined proposal is a hypothesis, not yet an improvement.
limits: Outer gate asks only non-regression, not improvement. Testbed size not given, so 'how large is enough' is not answered.
agent_relevance: A concrete recipe for gating memory writes: inner gate on source cases, outer gate on a fresh stratified held-out set by fault family, atomic promote, discard after 3 failed refinements.

source: OpsHarness (2026) gate ablation (RQ2)
finding: Without the gate, self-evolution first helps, then decays. Weak backbones overfit most. Example: the evolver up-weighted network anomalies after network failures, which then mislabelled CPU and memory cases that were right before.
numbers: Final-window A@1 averaged over 4 backbones: full 0.83, no-evolve 0.43, no-verify 0.33. DeepSeek-V4 no-verify fell from a peak 0.4 to 0.0. 37% of proposals rejected on average; accepted proposals need 1.7 attempts.
limits: Single paper, no peer review, no intervals shown. Gate on/off is the only ablation; gate size was not varied.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that ungated memory writes overfit and that damage is worse on weaker models. Do not claim a size threshold.

source: OpsHarness (2026) RQ1 distilled harness vs raw-trace ICL vs bare agent
finding: Distilled, evolved knowledge plus tools beats retrieving 3 raw correct rollouts (ICL) at about equal tokens. ICL barely beat the bare agent and hurt on some backbones.
numbers: Final A@1 over 4 backbones: OpsHarness 59.0, no-evolve 41.4, ICL 38.4, Direct 36.1, RCA-Agent 17.9, mABC 5.6. Avg tokens per case about 106k (OpsHarness), 112k (Direct), 106k (ICL). Per backbone: Codex ICL 45.3 vs Direct 51.2 on one sheet; Claude Code ICL 34.1 vs Direct 26.8.
limits: Not a pure text test: the harness also has a tool library and workflow skeleton. Test set is the last 20% in time of the same systems (OpenRCA 335 cases, RCAEval 270), so it is not novel fault families. No 'distilled text only' arm.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: distilled artifacts beat raw traces at equal cost on future cases of the same systems. A strategy-text-only arm and a novel-fault test are still missing.

source: OpsHarness (2026) which artifact families get used (Table III)
finding: Coarse artifacts are recalled broadly. Fine note-rules and persisted tools are recalled rarely but are right when they fire.
numbers: Workflow skeleton: 6 items, recall 91.7%, precision 73.5%. Operation skill: 19, 82.5%, 84.3%. Note-rule: 21, 64.7%, 85.1%. Persisted tool: 11, 61.0%, 77.2%.
limits: Recall and precision are descriptive co-occurrence, not causal. No ablation per family.
agent_relevance: Memory could hold a few workflow skeletons plus many small conditional rules; the small rules carry the precision.

source: Zha et al. (2026) Trace2Policy / EISR: iterative rule refinement with regression gate
finding: Distilling expert traces into a rule document once plateaus near 70%. Eight rounds of error-clustered patches, each kept only if it passes a regression gate, lift the same rules to about 79%. Domain is logistics damage auditing, not fault diagnosis.
numbers: Five-LLM averages: non-refinement baselines 70.3 / 73.3 / 69.2, EISR v8 78.9 action accuracy; category 55.0 vs 46.8 best baseline. 3,349 audit cases over 22 days. Auto-EISR costs 5-10 USD per 8-round run vs 70 expert-hours.
limits: Single domain, one carrier. Held-out sets are small (40 and 139 cases). Auto-EISR vs v1 on 139 cases: McNemar p=0.029, not significant after Bonferroni (alpha 0.025); Haiku p=0.071. Authors say a component ablation is missing.
agent_relevance: Supports 'refine distilled rules with an error loop and a gate' but not that it works for novel faults.

source: Zha et al. (2026) Trace2Policy authority displacement and held-out zero-shot
finding: Handing strong models unrefined distilled rules can make them worse than no rules. Weak models gain a lot. Refined rules close most of the gap.
numbers: On the 139-case held-out, unrefined v1 rules cut Opus and Haiku accuracy 7-9 points vs zero-shot (Opus zero-shot 82.7 vs v1 74.1 vs human-refined 77.2; Haiku 84.2 vs 77.0 vs 75.0). Weak Kimi gained 22.8 points.
quote: models deferring to explicit rules even when their own reasoning is superior
limits: Not diagnosis. Skewed base-rate compliance task. Human-refined v8 did not beat zero-shot action accuracy for the strong models.
agent_relevance: Counterpoint to gap 1: distilled strategy text can hurt a strong agent. Test it against a no-text arm, not only against raw traces. A recalled rule may be over-trusted.

source: Zha et al. (2026) Trace2Policy bypass test and gate settings
finding: A practitioner rewrite that skipped the gate (62 rules cut to a 4-rule tree) fell below every baseline. The automatic loop rolls back any patch that drops validation accuracy by more than 2%. In deployment the inference-time gate is switched off because it cost about 5 points of category accuracy.
numbers: v11 bypass: 66.8% validation, 67.5% held-out, below baseline B1b. Rollback rule: more than 2% drop. Round 5 crash 90% to 70% in training. In-sample 95% vs held-out 75%.
limits: Gate threshold chosen by authors, not tuned. Held-out sets of 40 and 139 cases are small, so a 2% threshold is within noise at those sizes.
agent_relevance: A gate needs a held-out set big enough that a 2-point change is measurable; 139 cases is not. Plan for several hundred.

source: Qi et al. (2026) R2Act: why valid recovery lags correct diagnosis
finding: Even when service and fault type are correctly diagnosed, models pick an invalid recovery action in 39.5-62.0% of cases (RAG LLMs) and 59.1-75.3% (zero/few-shot). The authors read this as an action-mapping problem, not missing diagnostic knowledge.
numbers: 302 incidents, 5-fold. Error taxonomy over 755 invalid predictions: wrong operation 513 (67.9%), invalid plan structure 224 (29.7%), wrong target or dependency 10 (1.3%), no-op 8 (1.1%). Gold RCA plus a fixed service/type-to-action mapper reaches only 0.599 validity. Qwen-RAG 99.0 RCA-service vs 48.0 recovery with full evidence; GLM-RAG 100 vs 61.9.
quote: many recovery failures arise not from missing diagnostic knowledge, but from the difficulty of translating diagnostic evidence into valid recovery actions
limits: One simulated microservice benchmark, one author group. 'Wrong operation' could be read as missing operational knowledge, so the 'not knowledge' reading is partly interpretive.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 mostly closed: the shortfall is operation and plan validity, not diagnosis. Add a typed action space and a precondition check before any repair step.

source: Qi et al. (2026) R2Act live replay and evidence ablation
finding: Offline validity matches live repair. More evidence helps weak methods but does not close the gap.
numbers: Replay of Qwen-RAG: 146 of 302 predictions offline-valid and recovered, 48.3%. CPU saturation, network delay and pod failure 100%; DNS 0.0% (plans omit the dependency target). NB recovery validity 6.6% (logs only) to 46.0% (full evidence).
limits: Replay re-injects Chaos Mesh faults with a 75-second health window. Only one model replayed.
agent_relevance: Direct repair checks (typed action, target, precondition) matter more than extra telemetry. Fault types needing dependency or configuration reasoning are where agents fail.

source: Fang et al. (2026) OpenRCA 2.0: process-level scoring of 11 LLMs
finding: Final answers hide ungrounded diagnoses. Agents name a correct service in most cases but draw a verified causal path in far fewer.
numbers: n=500, 11 models. AnySvc mean 76.0%; Path Reachability 61.5% (gap 14.5 points); strict recall 33.2%, EM 20.7%. Node F1 62.2% vs Edge F1 43.4% (18.8 points). Opus 4.7: AnySvc 82.6, PR 70.0, Edge F1 49.5.
limits: A benchmark paper: it measures, it does not train or select with the signal. Ground-truth paths come from injected-fault topology.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 only partly answered: closure scoring exposes failures, but nobody here shows it is a better training or selection signal than answer accuracy.

source: Fang et al. (2026) OpenRCA 2.0: ranking changes with grounding
finding: Models that look equal on outcome F1 differ in how often their right answer is grounded. The best model differs by column.
numbers: PR/AnySvc: Qwen3.6-Max 71.8/79.2 = about 91%; Sonnet 4.6 52.6/79.4 = about 66% with comparable F1. Column maxima fall on four different models. Per-system spread (TrainTicket 30+ point gap) exceeds cross-model spread.
limits: Whether grounding predicts later reliability is not tested.
agent_relevance: A selection signal based on grounding would rank models and runs differently from answer accuracy; whether it picks better ones is untested.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym controlled noise and first-anomaly greed
finding: With random transient noise injected, diagnosis falls for every agent-model pair. Trajectory reading shows all agents take the first plausible anomaly as the target, even when they saw evidence of the real fault.
numbers: Noise: two patterns every five minutes, two minutes each. Claude Code Sonnet-4.6 diagnosis 72.6% to 62.6%; Codex GPT-5.4 70.0% to 59.3%; Stratus Sonnet-4.6 61.5% to 51.5%. Mitigation is more robust to noise than diagnosis.
quote: they always treat the first plausible anomaly as the target failure (which can be a noise)
limits: Noise is ambient and unrelated, not a decoy built to look like the fault. No enumerate-alternatives arm. Trajectory claim is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 half answered: agents do show first-anomaly anchoring under injected noise. The remedy test (enumerate alternatives at equal tokens) is still missing.

source: Lu et al. (2026) failure-mode table: anchor lock and loudest-anomaly bias
finding: The coded failure modes include anchor lock (GEN1: early hypothesis kept against later contradictory evidence), salience bias (MIS2) and over-trusting the loudest anomaly (MIS3). Every mode is more common in wrong runs than right runs.
numbers: RCA100 baseline runs: incorrect runs show 3.29 distinct modes, correct runs 0.71. Listed rates: MIS3 42.0%; GEN1 28.0% and 34.6% in the two backbone columns by best reading. Table text is garbled in extraction, so the column assignment is uncertain.
limits: Codes were assigned to trajectories, not to a controlled decoy experiment. Re-check per-mode numbers against the PDF figure before citing.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is a common coded failure but its causal weight is unproven.

source: Lu et al. (2026) DiagGuard intervention (self-audit plus data grounding)
finding: A fixed Verifier (self-audit before the investigation and a soundness check before the verdict) plus a Grounder (search-space profile) raised Acc@1 in all 14 configs and cut modes per run.
numbers: Median gain +10.5 points (range 3.5-35.1) on 12 RCA100 configs; AIOps 2025 +6.5 and +9.0. mABC +21.1/+35.1 from baselines 35.1% and 3.5%. 1,368 coded runs (684 baseline, 684 DiagGuard). Modes per wrong run 3.29 to 2.82.
limits: Token cost not matched: the arms add prompt text and tools. Not an isolated enumerate-alternatives step. Same group built the taxonomy and the fix.
agent_relevance: Closest existing test for gap 4: self-audit that surfaces overlooked axes helps. A single-component, equal-token arm is still needed.

source: Luo et al. (2026) tool design for agentic RCA: keep or override the tool's candidate
finding: A tool candidate was right in over 80% of trajectories. Agents that gathered more evidence sometimes dropped it. Overrides outnumber corrections in every configuration. Checking the candidate with raw metrics helps; adding competing analysis hurts.
numbers: 375 failure cases, 3 systems. L1+L3: corrections 2.7% to 5.3%, overrides 4.2% to 5.8%. L2+L3: overrides 9.3%, corrections 3.8%. L3 82.8% vs L0 85.4% top-1 at under half the time. Qwen3-32B overrides nearly a third of its correct candidates.
limits: Qwen family only. Microservice RCA, so not the same as a human skill-to-knowledge switch.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: switching from a recalled or tool rule to model-based reasoning is not free. Default to the rule, switch only on a specific conflict check, and verify with raw evidence.

source: Katz et al. (1997) Hydrive vs F-15 tutor: what the two tutors differ in
finding: The two tutors differ in several things at once, so no single component (system model, strategy list, verify rule) can be isolated. Hydrive was built from a PARI task analysis and taught strategy and system knowledge. The comparison tutor came from one expert and taught procedures and a little system knowledge. Same scenarios.
numbers: Hydrive pre-post t(19)=4.14, p<.001; the other two groups showed no significant pre-post change. This is not a between-group test.
quote: only experts demonstrated the strategic knowledge that led to efficient and effective troubleshooting
limits: Confounded by developer, content and CTA method. Developers' own summary slides. No component ablation anywhere in the Sherlock/Hydrive set.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Three arms are needed: system model only, strategy list only, verify-before-act only, each at equal tokens.

source: Katz et al. (1997) Sherlock field evaluation sample sizes
finding: Field data show who was in each cell. There is no independent replication in this document.
numbers: Manual test station: tutored novices n=18, untutored n=23, masters n=13; about 20 hours over 3 weeks; VTT3 t[39]=-4.04, p<.001 and VIT4 t[39]=-3.72. Frankenstation: n=17, 21, 12; tutored vs untutored t[36]=-2.93, p<.01.
limits: Authors are the Sherlock developers. Small N. No later independent study was found in this session, but search quota ran out, so this is absence of evidence from limited search.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Treat the Sherlock effect sizes as one lab's result.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) personas in system prompts
finding: Adding a persona to the system prompt does not improve, and often lowers, accuracy on factual questions. Domain-aligned and work-related roles do slightly better; the best persona per question cannot be predicted.
numbers: 162 personas (interpersonal relationships and 8 expertise domains), 4 open model families, 2,410 factual questions. Domain classifier accuracy 78.1%.
limits: Factual questions only, open-weight models. No diagnosis or multi-step agent task. I did not find a diagnosis-specific persona test (search quota ran out).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Prior says a persona label is not expertise; a direct arm on fault tasks is still needed.

source: Cho et al. (2026) LLM-externalised tacit knowledge as guidance
finding: Notes written by an LLM from expert behaviour beat notes written by human experts in guiding a tutoring-response task, for a GPT-4o reader (Study 1) and for human novices (Study 2). A rigid three-step structure made the notes worse.
numbers: Study 1 (GPT-4o): ANOVA F(5,605)=35.01, p<.0001; vs experts' responses LLM+Conversation M=0.675 (p<.0001) and LLM+Both M=0.582 (p=.0004) higher. Study 2: 100 human novices per condition; gap to experts reduced by an estimated 0.517 points vs human-articulated notes (Tukey p<.01).
limits: Tutoring responses, not fault diagnosis. Quality scale and the exact contrast baseline are not fully clear from the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Support for gap 1 from an agent reader: distilled behaviour-derived guidance can lift a model on a held-out set of conversations. Fault tasks untested.

source: Borchers, Vie & Azevedo (2026) LLMs simulating novices
finding: GPT-4.1 asked to think aloud as a student is too coherent, too wordy and too confident, and overestimates learner success. Richer context made it worse. A 7B open model replicated it.
numbers: 630 human think-aloud utterances (chemistry tutoring). Richer context increased overestimation by about 0.14 (Welch t=5.01, p<.001).
limits: Simulating novices in text, not novice behaviour in action. Chemistry, not troubleshooting.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 context: LLMs do not naturally reproduce novice slips in text, yet agent runs do show them (SREGym, Lu). Anchoring is a search-policy issue, not role-play.

source: Wikipedia: Chunking (psychology), secondary summary of Chase and Simon 1973
finding: Secondary page only. It says skilled chess players encode larger chunks from brief views, and the gap shrinks a lot on random placements. It gives no recall numbers.
numbers: No figures on the page.
limits: Chase and Simon 1973 (ScienceDirect HTTP 403) and Chi et al. 1981 (Wiley Cloudflare challenge) primary texts were blocked and not opened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. The direction (pattern advantage shrinks on random positions) is the standard reading, not verified here.
